signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: What is the first question to ask when a patient presents with a rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: Not 'what is it called?' but 'is the patient systemically unwell, and are there red flags?' — screen for the dermatological emergencies before naming the rash.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: Which four rash presentations are emergencies to identify immediately?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: A non-blanching purpuric rash with fever (meningococcal sepsis), a painful rash with mucosal erosions and blistering/skin detachment (SJS/TEN), urticaria with airway/breathing compromise (anaphylaxis), and >90% body erythema (erythroderma).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: How do you demonstrate that a rash is non-blanching, and why does it matter?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: Press a glass slide over it; if it does not blanch, blood has leaked from the vessels (purpura). A non-blanching rash with fever is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: What features suggest Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: A painful rash with mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals), blistering, skin detachment and a positive Nikolsky sign, usually 1–3 weeks after a culprit drug; stop the drug urgently.
Gentle lateral pressure on the skin causes the epidermis to shear off; it is positive in SJS/TEN, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and pemphigus, indicating fragile epidermal adhesion.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: What is the systematic way to describe a rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: Site/distribution, configuration and arrangement, and morphology (macule, papule, vesicle, pustule, wheal, plaque, purpura), plus the time course and whether it itches or is painful.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: What is erythroderma and why is it dangerous?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: Erythema affecting >90% of the skin surface; it causes fluid, heat and protein loss, high-output cardiac failure and a risk of sepsis, and needs supportive care plus treatment of the underlying cause (eczema, psoriasis, drugs, lymphoma).

Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms — a widespread rash with fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and organ (often liver) involvement, typically 2–8 weeks after the culprit drug.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: How does eczema differ from psoriasis in distribution and morphology?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: Eczema is itchy, ill-defined and typically flexural (atopic); psoriasis has well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces, scalp and nails.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: What is eczema herpeticum and why is it important?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: Disseminated herpes simplex infection of eczematous skin, giving monomorphic punched-out erosions with systemic upset; it is a dermatological emergency requiring aciclovir.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: Which rash presentation should prompt an urgent look for necrotising fasciitis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: Rapidly spreading erythema with pain out of proportion to the skin signs, systemic toxicity and sometimes crepitus — it is a surgical emergency.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.front: What investigations are useful in a patient who is unwell with a rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.back: FBC, CRP, U&E, LFTs, blood cultures/meningococcal PCR and eosinophil count (DRESS); skin swab or viral PCR; a skin biopsy for blistering/uncertain rashes; and mast-cell tryptase after suspected anaphylaxis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: What is the single most useful division when assessing pruritus?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Whether there is a primary rash or not: itch WITH a rash is usually a skin disease; itch WITHOUT a rash (only excoriations) points to a systemic cause.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: Which skin diseases commonly cause pruritus with a rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Eczema, scabies, urticaria, lichen planus, dermatitis herpetiformis and bullous pemphigoid.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: Which systemic causes produce itch without a primary rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Cholestasis (obstructive jaundice, PBC), chronic kidney disease (uraemic), iron deficiency, thyroid disease, polycythaemia and lymphoma, malignancy (paraneoplastic), drugs (opioids), HIV and pregnancy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: What is the red-flag trio to look for in generalised pruritus?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Lymphadenopathy, jaundice and weight loss — pointing to lymphoma/malignancy or cholestatic obstruction.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: What does itch after a warm bath (aquagenic pruritus) suggest?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Polycythaemia vera; look for a ruddy complexion, splenomegaly and a raised haematocrit.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: How does Hodgkin lymphoma present with itch?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Generalised pruritus with B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fever), rubbery lymphadenopathy, and sometimes alcohol-induced node pain.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: Why does cholestasis cause itch, and what confirms it?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Retained bile salts deposit in the skin; cholestasis is confirmed by a raised ALP/GGT with a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and an ultrasound of the biliary tree.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: What is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and why does it matter?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Third-trimester itch (classically of the palms and soles) without a rash, with raised bile acids/LFTs; it carries a fetal risk (stillbirth) and is managed with monitoring and ursodeoxycholic acid.
Generalised itch in advanced chronic kidney disease/dialysis patients; it improves with optimised dialysis and treatment of associated factors (e.g. hyperphosphataemia).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: What investigations are appropriate for itch without a rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: FBC and film, ferritin, U&E/eGFR, LFTs (ALP/GGT), TFTs, glucose, LDH and an HIV test; bile acids in pregnancy; imaging ± lymph-node biopsy if lymphoma is suspected.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: What is the commonest cause of generalised itch in the elderly?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Xerosis (dry skin), which is worse in winter and with frequent washing; it responds to emollients.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.front: What are the general symptomatic measures for pruritus?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.back: Emollients, cooling/avoiding heat, avoiding soap and hot baths, and antihistamines (sedating ones at night), while treating the underlying cause.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.front: What defines a purpuric rash and how is it demonstrated?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.back: It is non-blanching — blood has leaked into the skin; pressing a glass slide over it does not make it disappear (the tumbler test).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.front: What is the key dermatological morphological classification of purpura?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.back: Non-palpable (macular), palpable, or retiform/necrotic — each pointing to a different mechanism (platelet/vessel, vasculitis, or occlusion respectively).

Inflammation of the vessel wall — a small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis such as Henoch-Schönlein purpura, drug- or infection-related vasculitis, or ANCA-associated/cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.front: What does retiform (net-like) or necrotic purpura indicate?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.back: Vessel occlusion — DIC/purpura fulminans, warfarin skin necrosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, calciphylaxis or cholesterol emboli.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.front: What are the causes of non-palpable purpura?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.back: Thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy/anticoagulants, and fragile vessels (senile, actinic and steroid purpura, scurvy, trauma, amyloid).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.front: What is the reflex rule for any purpuric rash with fever?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.back: Fever with a non-blanching (purpuric) rash in an unwell patient is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise — give immediate antibiotics without waiting.
Palpable purpura over the buttocks and extensor legs with abdominal pain, arthralgia and nephritis (haematuria/proteinuria), usually in a child and often post-infectious.
Retiform/necrotic purpura developing a few days after starting warfarin, due to a transient procoagulant state (protein C depletion); it needs warfarin withdrawal and anticoagulation cover.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.front: Which investigations are used for palpable purpura?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.back: A skin biopsy (showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis), ANCA, complement and cryoglobulins, plus urinalysis and renal function to assess for glomerulonephritis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.front: Which cutaneous signs of infective endocarditis can appear as purpura?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.back: Splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions and Osler's nodes, with fever and a new or changing murmur.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.front: Which investigations are used when purpura is non-palpable?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.back: FBC and blood film (platelets, blasts, schistocytes) and a coagulation screen; a low platelet count points to thrombocytopenia, deranged clotting to a coagulopathy, and normal results to fragile-vessel purpura.
Non-palpable purpura on the backs of the hands and extensor forearms in an elderly or steroid-treated patient, with a normal platelet count and clotting.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: Transient, itchy, raised wheals — each individual lesion lasts less than 24 hours, blanches and migrates; it may be accompanied by angioedema (deeper swelling of lips, tongue, eyelids or genitals).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: What is the first thing to exclude in a patient with urticaria?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: Anaphylaxis — wheals with airway, breathing or circulatory compromise (lip/tongue swelling, wheeze, stridor, hypotension) require immediate IM adrenaline.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: How is urticaria classified by time course?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: Acute (less than 6 weeks) — usually allergic (food, drug, sting) or post-viral; and chronic (more than 6 weeks) — spontaneous (autoimmune/idiopathic) or inducible (physical).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: What are the types of chronic inducible (physical) urticaria?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: Dermographism, cold urticaria, cholinergic urticaria (heat/exercise/sweat), delayed pressure urticaria, solar urticaria and aquagenic urticaria; each is confirmed by provocation testing.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: What distinguishes urticarial vasculitis from ordinary urticaria?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: In urticarial vasculitis individual weals last more than 24 hours, are painful/burning rather than itchy, and resolve leaving bruising or pigmentation; a skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: Which systemic conditions are associated with urticarial vasculitis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: Connective tissue disease (especially SLE), hepatitis and (via low complement) systemic vasculitis; check complement and ANA.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: Why is angioedema without weals important to recognise?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: It suggests ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema or hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase-inhibitor deficiency), which can cause laryngeal oedema and do not respond well to antihistamines.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: How is hereditary angioedema diagnosed and what points to it?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: Recurrent angioedema without weals, often with a family history and abdominal attacks; diagnosed by a low C1-esterase inhibitor level/function and a low C4.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: What is the first-line treatment of chronic spontaneous urticaria?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: Regular non-sedating antihistamines (up-dosed to four times the standard dose if needed), stepping up to omalizumab in refractory cases.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: Which common drugs precipitate or worsen urticaria/angioedema?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: NSAIDs and aspirin, ACE inhibitors (angioedema), and antibiotics such as penicillins (IgE-mediated allergy).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.front: What investigations are appropriate in chronic urticaria?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.back: Often none; consider FBC, ESR/CRP and thyroid function/antibodies for chronic spontaneous urticaria, provocation tests for inducible urticaria, and C1-inhibitor/C4 for angioedema without weals.
A form of inducible urticaria in which linear wheals appear where the skin is stroked or scratched.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: Redness and scaling affecting more than 90% of the skin surface; it is a dermatological emergency regardless of the underlying cause.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: Why is erythroderma a medical emergency?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: The failing skin barrier causes fluid and electrolyte loss, temperature dysregulation (hypothermia), high-output cardiac failure, hypoalbuminaemia/oedema and secondary infection/sepsis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: What are the classic five causes of erythroderma?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: Eczema, psoriasis, drug reactions, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sézary syndrome) and idiopathic.
The leukaemic/erythrodermic form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma — erythroderma with lymphadenopathy and circulating atypical (Sézary) cells in the blood.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: How does a drug cause erythroderma, and what is DRESS?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: Drugs (e.g. anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides) can cause exfoliative erythroderma; DRESS is Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms — rash with fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia and organ (liver) involvement.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: What can precipitate erythrodermic psoriasis in a known psoriatic patient?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: Abrupt withdrawal of systemic (or potent topical) steroids, infection, drugs, or a phototherapy burn.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: What clue suggests pityriasis rubra pilaris as the cause of erythroderma?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: Islands of sparing (unaffected skin within the erythroderma), orange-red palms and soles, and follicular hyperkeratotic papules.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: What immediate supportive measures does erythroderma need?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: Admission with warming, rehydration and electrolyte/albumin correction, treatment of infection, bland emollients/wet wraps, and stopping any culprit drug.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: What investigations help find the cause of erythroderma?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: FBC (eosinophils, Sézary cells), U&E, albumin, LFTs, CRP and cultures; a skin biopsy (with T-cell clonality if lymphoma suspected); and a peripheral blood film/flow cytometry.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: Which two causes of erythroderma must not be missed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma/Sézary syndrome, and a drug reaction/DRESS (stop the culprit drug).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: What cardiac complication can erythroderma precipitate?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: High-output cardiac failure, due to widespread cutaneous vasodilation increasing the circulatory demand.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.front: How is idiopathic erythroderma ('red man syndrome') diagnosed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma.back: It is a diagnosis of exclusion, made when no cause is identified despite history, examination, biopsy and investigations; many later declare an underlying dermatosis or lymphoma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: How are blisters classified by size?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: Vesicles are small blisters (less than 5 mm) and bullae are large blisters (more than 5 mm).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: What is the key bedside distinction between the immunobullous diseases?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: Tense vs flaccid blisters and the Nikolsky sign: bullous pemphigoid is tense (subepidermal, Nikolsky negative); pemphigus vulgaris is flaccid with mucosal involvement and a positive Nikolsky (intraepidermal).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: What features indicate Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN in a blistering rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: Skin pain, mucosal erosions (mouth, eyes, genitals), sheets of skin detachment and a positive Nikolsky sign, usually 1–3 weeks after a culprit drug.
Disseminated herpes simplex infection of eczematous skin, producing monomorphic punched-out vesicles/erosions with systemic upset; it needs urgent aciclovir.
Tense, itchy bullae on an erythematous base in an elderly patient, usually sparing the mucosa; biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: How does pemphigus vulgaris present and why is it dangerous?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: Flaccid bullae that rupture into painful erosions with prominent mucosal involvement and a positive Nikolsky sign; it can be life-threatening from fluid loss and sepsis, and needs immunosuppression.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: What is dermatitis herpetiformis and what is it associated with?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: Intensely itchy grouped vesicles on the extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks) associated with coeliac disease; biopsy shows granular IgA, and it responds to a gluten-free diet and dapsone.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: How does herpes zoster (shingles) present as a blistering rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: Painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution that do not cross the midline, often with preceding pain; treated with antivirals (aciclovir).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: Which investigation confirms the immunobullous diseases?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: A skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence (plus serum anti-desmoglein antibodies for pemphigus and anti-BP180 for pemphigoid).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: What is staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: A toxin-mediated superficial blistering/peeling of the skin (Nikolsky positive), typically in young children, requiring antibiotics and supportive care.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: Which metabolic condition causes photodistributed skin fragility and blistering?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: Porphyria cutanea tarda, with blistering and skin fragility on sun-exposed areas, hypertrichosis and often associated liver disease/hepatitis C.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.front: What is the general management approach to a blistering rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash.back: Treat the emergency first (stop the drug and give burns care for SJS/TEN, aciclovir for eczema herpeticum, antibiotics for infection), then treat the specific cause (immunosuppression for pemphigus/pemphigoid, gluten-free diet plus dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis), with wound care and analgesia throughout.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: What is the single most important question when assessing alopecia?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: Is it scarring (cicatricial) or non-scarring? Scarring alopecia (loss of follicular openings) is permanent and needs an urgent scalp biopsy; non-scarring is potentially reversible.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: How do you distinguish scarring from non-scarring alopecia at the bedside?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: Look at the scalp: in scarring alopecia the follicular openings are lost and the scalp is smooth/shiny/inflamed; in non-scarring alopecia the follicular openings are preserved.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: Name the main causes of scarring (cicatricial) alopecia.
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: Lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus erythematosus, folliculitis decalvans and frontal fibrosing alopecia.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: What are the classic features of alopecia areata?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: Smooth, round bald patches with preserved follicles, exclamation-mark hairs at the margins, and nail pitting; it is autoimmune and may progress to alopecia totalis/universalis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: How does tinea capitis present and why must it be treated?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: A scaly patch with broken hairs in a child (may fluoresce under Wood's lamp); a boggy inflammatory kerion can scar, so it needs oral antifungals.
Diffuse hair shedding occurring about 3 months after a trigger (severe illness, surgery, childbirth, major stress, crash diet); it is reversible once the trigger resolves.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: Which systemic/metabolic causes produce diffuse non-scarring hair loss?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: Thyroid disease, iron deficiency, drugs (chemotherapy, retinoids, anticoagulants), protein-calorie malnutrition and SLE.
Patterned hair loss from follicular miniaturisation — bitemporal recession and vertex thinning in men, and a widened central part in women; treated with topical minoxidil (± finasteride in men).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: Which investigations are appropriate in diffuse hair loss?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: Thyroid function tests and ferritin (± FBC), a drug history, and an autoimmune screen (ANA) where lupus is suspected.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: What investigation is required for scarring alopecia?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: An urgent scalp biopsy, because early treatment can halt progression and save the remaining hair.
Hair loss caused by repetitive pulling, producing irregular patches with broken hairs of varying lengths; it is a non-scarring cause.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.front: What clue points to lupus as a cause of scarring alopecia?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia.back: Scarring scalp plaques with a photosensitive facial (malar) rash and scaly discoid plaques; check ANA.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.front: How should nails be examined systematically?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.back: Assess shape, colour, surface, the nail fold and the free edge, in all nails, and decide whether a change affects one digit or is symmetrical across many.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.front: What nail change must never be dismissed, and why?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.back: A single-digit longitudinal pigmented band that widens/is irregular or shows Hutchinson's sign (pigment spreading onto the nail fold) — it is a subungual melanoma until biopsy proves otherwise.
Extension of nail pigment onto the adjacent nail fold/periungual skin, a warning sign of subungual melanoma.

Loss of the nail-fold angle with a fluctuant nail bed; it is never normal and indicates underlying disease — lung cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, cyanotic congenital heart disease, IBD or cirrhosis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.front: What do splinter haemorrhages suggest in the right clinical context?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.back: With fever and a new murmur they suggest infective endocarditis; they can also result from vasculitis or (commonly) trauma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.front: What nail changes are characteristic of psoriasis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.back: Pitting, onycholysis, the 'oil-drop' sign (salmon patch), and subungual hyperkeratosis; pitting also occurs in alopecia areata and eczema.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.front: What is koilonychia and what does it indicate?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.back: Spoon-shaped nails, classically indicating iron-deficiency anaemia.
Hypoalbuminaemia, classically from chronic liver disease (or nephrotic syndrome/malnutrition).
Transverse ridges/grooves across the nails reflecting a temporary arrest of nail growth during a severe systemic illness.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.front: What nailfold sign suggests connective tissue disease?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.back: Nailfold telangiectasia/dilated capillary loops (seen on capillaroscopy), especially with Raynaud's phenomenon, in systemic sclerosis or dermatomyositis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.front: How does onychomycosis (fungal nail infection) appear?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.back: A thickened, discoloured (yellow), crumbly nail with subungual debris; confirmed by nail clipping microscopy and fungal culture.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.front: What is the significance of symmetrical versus single-digit nail changes?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes.back: Symmetrical changes across many nails point to a systemic cause; a change in a single digit (especially a pigmented band) raises melanoma or local disease.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: What is the core question for any pigmented skin lesion?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: Could this be a melanoma? Screen with the ABCDE rule and the ugly-duckling sign, and act on any history of change.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: What does the ABCDE rule stand for?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, more than one Colour, Diameter greater than 6 mm, and Evolving/changing (the most important feature).
A mole that looks different from (stands out among) the patient's other moles, raising suspicion of melanoma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: What is nodular melanoma and why is it dangerous?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: A rapidly growing, firm, elevated nodule (EFG: Elevated, Firm, Growing) that may be amelanotic (pink); it is aggressive and can be missed because it lacks classic pigment.
A slowly enlarging pigmented macule on chronically sun-damaged skin (typically the face of an elderly patient), which is melanoma in situ and can progress to invasive melanoma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: Which melanomas occur at special sites that are easily missed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: Acral melanoma (palms and soles) and subungual melanoma (a single-nail pigmented band with Hutchinson's sign); also mucosal melanoma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: Why should a suspected melanoma be excised rather than shave-biopsied?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: Because the Breslow thickness (depth of invasion) determines prognosis and management, and needs the full-thickness lesion for accurate measurement.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: How does a seborrhoeic keratosis appear?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: A well-defined, 'stuck-on', warty, greasy plaque, often pigmented; it is benign and looks as if it could be picked off the skin.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: What are the features of a benign melanocytic naevus?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: Symmetry, a regular border, uniform colour, small stable size and no change over time.
A firm benign dermal nodule (often on the leg) that dimples inward when pinched (the 'dimple sign').

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: Which referral pathway applies to a suspicious pigmented lesion?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: An urgent (2-week-wait) referral for dermoscopy and excision biopsy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.front: What features in the history increase the risk that a pigmented lesion is melanoma?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion.back: Change in size/shape/colour, bleeding, itching or a new lesion in an adult, plus risk factors (fair skin, sunburn/sunbed use, many moles, personal/family history of melanoma, immunosuppression).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: What are the three common vascular causes of leg ulcers?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: Venous (most common, ~70%), arterial, and neuropathic ulcers — assessed with the ABPI and covered in the vascular leg-ulcers note.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: When should a leg ulcer be regarded as 'atypical' and investigated further?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: When it is in an unusual site, has an atypical edge (rolled or undermined), is disproportionately painful, is rapidly growing, or fails to heal despite correct treatment.
A squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound, scar or long-standing ulcer; it shows a rolled/everted edge and non-healing, and needs an edge biopsy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: What are the features of pyoderma gangrenosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: A rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a violaceous, undermined border and pathergy (worsening with trauma/debridement); it is associated with IBD, rheumatoid arthritis and myeloproliferative disease.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: Why must debridement be avoided in pyoderma gangrenosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: Because of pathergy — trauma (including surgical debridement) worsens the ulcer; treatment is immunosuppression plus management of the underlying disease.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: What suggests a vasculitic leg ulcer?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: Painful, punched-out ulcers on a background of livedo reticularis or palpable purpura, with systemic features; confirmed by skin biopsy and ANCA/autoantibodies.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: What is the key investigation before applying compression to a leg ulcer?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: The ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI), to exclude significant arterial disease (compression is unsafe if the ABPI is low).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: Which investigation confirms a malignant leg ulcer?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: An edge (or wedge) biopsy of the ulcer for histology.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: Which systemic/haematological condition causes leg ulcers in young patients?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: Sickle cell disease, classically causing malleolar ulcers.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: What features on examination help classify a leg ulcer?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: The site (gaiter vs atypical), the edge (sloping/punched-out/rolled/undermined), the base and exudate, the surrounding skin (venous changes, livedo, purpura, cellulitis), and the pulses and neurology.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: What is the significance of an ulcer that fails to heal despite appropriate treatment?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: It should raise suspicion of an atypical cause (malignancy, pyoderma gangrenosum, vasculitis or infection) and prompt a biopsy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.front: What investigations are appropriate for an atypical leg ulcer?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers.back: ABPI/Doppler, an edge biopsy, wound swab/tissue culture (including AFB and fungal), and bloods (FBC, CRP, ANCA, autoantibodies, glucose/HbA1c, haemoglobinopathy screen).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: What is the diagnostic hallmark of a photosensitive rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: Its photodistribution: it affects sun-exposed sites (face, V of the neck, dorsal hands, extensor forearms) and characteristically spares shaded areas (under the chin, behind the ears, the upper eyelids and skin under clothing).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: What is the commonest cause of photosensitivity?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: Drug-induced (phototoxic or photoallergic) photosensitivity — e.g. doxycycline, thiazides, amiodarone, NSAIDs, quinolones and retinoids; it is reversible on stopping the drug.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: Which connective tissue diseases present with a photosensitive rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: Lupus erythematosus (malar/discoid rash) and dermatomyositis (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: What are the cutaneous features of dermatomyositis, and why is it important in adults?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: A heliotrope (violaceous) eyelid rash, Gottron's papules over the knuckles, and the shawl/V sign, with proximal muscle weakness; in adults it is often paraneoplastic, so a malignancy screen is required.
The commonest idiopathic photodermatosis — itchy papules/vesicles appearing hours after sun exposure, typically in young women in spring, improving with continued exposure ('hardening').

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: How does porphyria cutanea tarda present?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: Skin fragility, blistering, milia and hypertrichosis on sun-exposed skin (especially the dorsal hands), often associated with alcohol, hepatitis C or haemochromatosis.
Burning and stinging of the skin within minutes of sun exposure, typically starting in childhood, often without obvious rash.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: Which investigations confirm lupus as the cause of a photosensitive rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: ANA, anti-Ro/La and anti-dsDNA antibodies, with a skin biopsy where needed.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: What nutritional deficiency causes a photosensitive dermatitis, and what is its sign?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: Niacin deficiency (pellagra), producing a photosensitive dermatitis of the neck (Casal's necklace) with diarrhoea and dementia.
Urinary, plasma and red-cell porphyrin levels.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: What is the cornerstone of management for all photosensitive rashes?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: Photoprotection — broad-spectrum high-SPF sunscreen, protective clothing and sun avoidance — alongside treating the specific cause.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.front: How can the timing of the rash after sun exposure help diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Ra.back: Minutes (solar urticaria, erythropoietic protoporphyria), hours (polymorphic light eruption), and delayed/persistent (drug-induced or lupus).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.front: Why is the distribution of a facial rash so important?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.back: On the face, the site involved (central, nasolabial folds, eyelids, a dermatome) plus the morphology usually points directly to the diagnosis.

Orbital cellulitis (proptosis, painful eye movements, reduced acuity), herpes zoster ophthalmicus (V1 shingles with Hutchinson's sign), and angioedema (lip/periorbital swelling threatening the airway).
A sharply demarcated, raised, hot, red, tender area of facial swelling with fever (a superficial streptococcal cellulitis).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.front: What is Hutchinson's sign in herpes zoster ophthalmicus?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.back: A vesicle on the tip (or side) of the nose, indicating nasociliary (V1) nerve involvement and a high risk of eye involvement; it requires antivirals and urgent ophthalmology.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.front: How does rosacea differ from acne?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.back: Rosacea shows central facial flushing, papulopustules and telangiectasia with NO comedones; acne has comedones (blackheads/whiteheads) plus papulopustules.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.front: Where does seborrhoeic dermatitis characteristically affect the face?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.back: The nasolabial folds, eyebrows, glabella and scalp, with greasy scaling (associated with Malassezia).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.front: How does the malar rash of lupus differ from seborrhoeic dermatitis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.back: The lupus butterfly rash spares the nasolabial folds, is photosensitive and comes with systemic features; seborrhoeic dermatitis favours the nasolabial folds.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.front: What are the facial signs of dermatomyositis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.back: A heliotrope (violaceous) rash of the eyelids and Gottron's papules over the knuckles, with proximal muscle weakness; in adults it may be paraneoplastic.
Papules and pustules around the mouth sparing the vermilion border, often related to topical steroid use; treated by stopping steroids and using topical/oral antibiotics.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.front: Which investigations are used for an eye-threatening facial rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.back: CT of the orbits with bloods/cultures for orbital cellulitis, and urgent ophthalmology assessment for herpes zoster ophthalmicus.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.front: What is the general management approach to a facial rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash.back: Treat any emergency first (IV antibiotics for orbital cellulitis, antivirals plus ophthalmology for zoster ophthalmicus, adrenaline/airway care for angioedema), then treat the specific inflammatory pattern.
Sun, heat, alcohol, spicy food and stress; avoidance is part of management.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: A reactive septal panniculitis presenting as tender, red, raised subcutaneous nodules, typically bilateral on the shins, that do not ulcerate and fade like bruises.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: Why is erythema nodosum described as 'a sign, not a disease'?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: It is a hypersensitivity reaction to an underlying trigger, so recognising it should prompt a search for the cause.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: What is the commonest identifiable cause of erythema nodosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: Streptococcal infection (especially in children), often following a sore throat, with a raised ASO titre.
The combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, arthralgia and fever — an acute presentation of sarcoidosis with a good prognosis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: Which serious infection must be excluded in erythema nodosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: Tuberculosis (erythema nodosum can be a hypersensitivity reaction to TB); screen with a chest X-ray and IGRA.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: Which gastrointestinal disease is associated with erythema nodosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: Which drugs and physiological state can trigger erythema nodosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: Sulfonamides, penicillins and the combined oral contraceptive pill; and pregnancy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: What is the core investigation panel for erythema nodosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: Chest X-ray, FBC and CRP/ESR, ASO titre and throat swab, IGRA (for TB), serum ACE and calcium (sarcoid), and faecal calprotectin (± endoscopy) for IBD, plus a drug and pregnancy history.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: How is erythema nodosum itself managed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: Rest, leg elevation and NSAIDs; the nodules are self-limiting over weeks, and management is otherwise directed at the underlying cause.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: Which rheumatological condition causes erythema nodosum with oral and genital ulcers and uveitis?
What proportion of erythema nodosum cases are idiopathic?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: Up to about a third, where no cause is found despite investigation.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.front: What are the key examination features that identify erythema nodosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum.back: Tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules on the shins, usually bilateral, that do not ulcerate and evolve/fade like bruises.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: A neutrophilic dermatosis presenting as a rapidly enlarging, exquisitely painful ulcer with a characteristic violaceous, overhanging, undermined border, often starting as a pustule or nodule.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: What is pathergy and why does it matter in pyoderma gangrenosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: Pathergy is worsening of the lesion with trauma; in PG, debridement, surgery or grafting can cause dramatic enlargement, so the ulcer must NOT be debrided.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: Why is pyoderma gangrenosum called a diagnosis of exclusion?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: Because a rapidly progressive ulcer can also be infection, vasculitis or malignancy, which must be excluded with an edge biopsy and tissue cultures before treating as PG.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: What is the mainstay of treatment for pyoderma gangrenosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: Immunosuppression — potent topical/intralesional or systemic corticosteroids, ciclosporin, or a TNF inhibitor — with analgesia and gentle wound care (not debridement).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: What is the commonest systemic association of pyoderma gangrenosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis); peristomal PG around a stoma is characteristic.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: Which rheumatological and haematological conditions are associated with PG?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: Rheumatoid and seronegative arthritis; and haematological disease such as myeloma/IgA gammopathy, leukaemia and myelodysplasia.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: What does biopsy show in pyoderma gangrenosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: A neutrophilic infiltrate, which is supportive but not specific; the main value of biopsy is to exclude infection, vasculitis and malignancy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: Which investigations screen for the associations of PG?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: FBC and blood film, ESR/CRP, faecal calprotectin (± endoscopy) for IBD, RF/anti-CCP for rheumatoid arthritis, and serum electrophoresis for a paraprotein.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: What is the classic clinical error in managing pyoderma gangrenosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: Mistaking it for infection and debriding it, which worsens the ulcer through pathergy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: Where does pyoderma gangrenosum most commonly occur?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: The lower legs, and around stomas (peristomal PG); it can occur at sites of trauma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: Which additional investigations exclude the main mimics of PG?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: Tissue cultures (bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal) to exclude infection, and biopsy plus ANCA to exclude vasculitis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.front: What are the recognised variants of pyoderma gangrenosum?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangreno.back: Classic ulcerative, bullous, pustular, vegetative and peristomal variants; PG is also part of the PAPA autoinflammatory syndrome.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: What is the defining lesion of erythema multiforme?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: The target (iris) lesion — concentric rings with a dusky or blistered centre — distributed acrally on the extensor limbs, palms, soles and face.
EM minor (little or no mucosal involvement) and EM major (mucosal involvement of the eyes, mouth and/or genitals).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: What is the commonest trigger of erythema multiforme?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: Herpes simplex virus infection, which is also the usual cause of recurrent EM (often preceded by a cold sore).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: Which infection commonly triggers mucosal-predominant erythema multiforme in children?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (giving 'mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis', MIRM), typically after a respiratory illness.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: How is erythema multiforme distinguished from SJS/TEN?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: EM has typical acral target lesions, is usually infection-triggered and has a good prognosis; SJS/TEN is drug-induced with widespread dusky/atypical macules, prominent skin pain, blistering and detachment, and a far worse prognosis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: How is recurrent erythema multiforme managed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: By treating/suppressing the trigger — usually suppressive antiviral therapy for HSV-driven recurrent EM.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: What does EM major with ocular involvement require?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: Ophthalmology assessment to prevent scarring, plus fluids and mouth/eye care.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: Which drugs can (less commonly) cause erythema multiforme?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: Sulfonamides, NSAIDs, anticonvulsants and penicillins — though drug causes should prompt reconsideration of SJS/TEN if the picture is widespread and painful.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: What investigations are used in erythema multiforme?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: It is largely clinical; consider HSV PCR/serology, mycoplasma serology/PCR (± chest X-ray), and a skin biopsy if the diagnosis is uncertain or SJS/TEN is suspected.
Symptomatic care (antihistamines, topical steroids) and treatment of the trigger; it is self-limiting over about two weeks.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: Where are target lesions of erythema multiforme typically distributed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: Acrally — on the extensor surfaces of the limbs, the palms and soles, and the face.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.front: What preceding history commonly points to the trigger of EM?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multifor.back: A cold sore 1–2 weeks before (HSV) or a preceding cough/atypical pneumonia in a child (mycoplasma).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Erythema across the cheeks and the bridge of the nose in a butterfly distribution.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: What is the single most useful sign distinguishing lupus from its facial mimics?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Whether the nasolabial folds are spared: the acute cutaneous lupus of SLE spares the nasolabial folds, whereas seborrhoeic dermatitis and rosacea favour them.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: What features accompany the malar rash of SLE?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: It is photosensitive and non-scarring, with systemic features such as arthralgia, mouth ulcers, hair loss, serositis and renal/haematological disease.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: Which investigations confirm SLE as the cause of a malar rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: ANA, anti-dsDNA and ENA antibodies, complement (C3/C4), FBC, U&E with urinalysis, and a skin biopsy where needed.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: How does rosacea differ from the malar rash of lupus?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Rosacea causes central facial flushing, papulopustules and telangiectasia, involves the nasolabial folds, and has no systemic autoimmune features.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: How does seborrhoeic dermatitis present on the face?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Greasy scaling of the nasolabial folds, eyebrows and scalp (favouring the folds, unlike lupus).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: What are the facial signs of dermatomyositis, and why is it important?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: A heliotrope (violaceous) eyelid rash and Gottron's papules with proximal muscle weakness; in adults it is often paraneoplastic, requiring a malignancy screen.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: What causes a 'slapped cheek' appearance in a child?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Parvovirus B19 infection (erythema infectiosum/fifth disease), often with a lacy body rash.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: How is erysipelas of the face distinguished from a malar rash of lupus?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Erysipelas is a sharply demarcated, hot, tender, febrile red swelling (an infection), not a photosensitive autoimmune rash.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: What is discoid lupus and how does it differ from acute cutaneous lupus?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Discoid lupus causes scarring plaques with scale and follicular plugging, whereas the acute cutaneous (malar) lupus rash is non-scarring.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: Why must a malar rash prompt consideration of systemic disease?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Because it can be the presenting sign of SLE or dermatomyositis, both of which have important systemic and (for dermatomyositis) malignancy associations.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).front: What management applies to lupus/dermatomyositis-related malar rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly).back: Referral and immunosuppression (treating any underlying malignancy in dermatomyositis), together with strict photoprotection.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: A netlike, violaceous mottling of the skin caused by sluggish flow/obstruction in the dermal vascular network.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.front: What is the key distinction when assessing livedo?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: Whether it is reversible (physiological cutis marmorata — a fine, complete, symmetrical net that warms out) or fixed/broken (livedo racemosa — pathological).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.front: What is livedo racemosa and why does it matter?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: A larger, broken, irregular livedo pattern that persists on warming; it signals vessel occlusion or inflammation and warrants investigation.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.front: Which thrombotic condition classically causes livedo with stroke?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: Antiphospholipid syndrome (Sneddon's syndrome is livedo plus stroke); check antiphospholipid antibodies.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.front: How does cholesterol embolism present with livedo?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: Livedo with blue toes, renal impairment and eosinophilia, typically after angiography, vascular surgery or anticoagulation.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.front: How does polyarteritis nodosa present with livedo?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: Livedo racemosa with subcutaneous nodules, mononeuritis multiplex, hypertension and renal disease (a medium-vessel vasculitis, associated with hepatitis B).
Physiological livedo — a fine, complete, symmetrical net that reverses with warming, common in infants and in cold conditions; it is benign.
Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies (persistently positive).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.front: Which connective tissue disease commonly causes livedo?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: Systemic lupus erythematosus (also dermatomyositis and systemic sclerosis).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.front: What investigations are appropriate for fixed (racemosa) livedo?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: Antiphospholipid antibodies, FBC (eosinophils), U&E and urinalysis, ANA/ENA/complement, coagulation screen, cryoglobulins and hepatitis B, plus a skin biopsy and/or angiography where PAN or emboli are suspected.
Anticoagulation (once the syndrome is confirmed), alongside management of thrombotic events.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.front: Which other conditions can cause livedo?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticulari.back: DIC, cryoglobulinaemia, hyperviscosity/thrombophilia, calciphylaxis (in renal failure), sepsis and certain drugs (e.g. amantadine).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: What are the classic features of a basal cell carcinoma (BCC)?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: A pearly/translucent papule with surface telangiectasia, a rolled edge and central ulceration (a rodent ulcer); it is slow-growing and locally destructive but rarely metastasises.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: What are the classic features of a squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: A keratotic, crusted, ulcerated, tender nodule that grows over weeks; it can metastasise, especially on the lip/ear, in a scar, or in immunosuppressed patients.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: Which factors make an SCC 'high-risk' for metastasis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: Location on the lip or ear, large size, poor differentiation, arising in a scar/chronic wound, and immunosuppression (e.g. organ transplant).
A rough, scaly, sandpapery patch on chronically sun-damaged skin; a pre-malignant lesion with a small risk of progression to SCC.
Squamous cell carcinoma in situ — a slow-growing, well-demarcated scaly erythematous plaque (often on the lower leg).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: What is a keratoacanthoma and how is it managed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: A rapidly growing dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug; it is treated as an SCC (excision) because the two can be difficult to distinguish.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: Which lesions should always prompt an urgent (2-week-wait) referral?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: A new, growing, ulcerating, bleeding or non-healing lesion, a suspected SCC, and any lesion suspicious for melanoma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: How is a suspected melanoma distinguished from a keratinocyte cancer, and why does it matter?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: Melanoma is assessed with ABCDE and the ugly-duckling sign (and may be amelanotic); it is excised (not shaved) to measure Breslow thickness, and it carries a higher metastatic risk.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: What is the definitive investigation for a suspicious BCC or SCC?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: A diagnostic biopsy or definitive surgical excision for histology (with staging for high-risk/metastatic SCC).
Cryotherapy or field therapy with topical 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod, plus sun protection.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: Which treatment is used for high-risk facial BCC/SCC?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: Mohs micrographic surgery, which allows margin-controlled excision while sparing tissue.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.front: What preventive advice applies to patients with keratinocyte skin cancers?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin L.back: Sun protection (sunscreen, clothing, avoidance) and surveillance, particularly in high-risk (e.g. immunosuppressed) patients.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: What two questions must be answered when a patient has hot, tender, spreading erythema?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: First, is there a necrotising infection or sepsis? Second, is it really cellulitis (rather than one of its mimics)?

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: What features suggest necrotising fasciitis rather than cellulitis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: Pain out of proportion to the skin signs, rapid spread, crepitus, dusky skin/haemorrhagic bullae/necrosis, and systemic toxicity; it is a surgical emergency.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: What are the typical features of true cellulitis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: Unilateral, hot, tender, poorly demarcated spreading erythema with fever and a portal of entry (tinea, wound, ulcer); usually streptococcal or staphylococcal.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: How does erysipelas differ from cellulitis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: Erysipelas is more superficial and sharply demarcated with a raised edge (classically streptococcal).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: Why is cellulitis often over-diagnosed, and what is the commonest mimic?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: Bilateral, chronic, itchy lower-leg redness is usually venous eczema (stasis dermatitis), not infection — the commonest misdiagnosis of cellulitis.
Venous eczema, DVT, acute gout, contact dermatitis and erythema migrans (Lyme disease).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: What immediate management does necrotising fasciitis require?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: Urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics (and resuscitation); it must not be delayed for imaging.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: What should you do when spreading erythema is accompanied by fever, tachycardia and hypotension?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: Recognise sepsis and start the Sepsis 6 (cultures, lactate, antibiotics, IV fluids, oxygen, monitor urine output), with source control.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: How is cellulitis investigated and monitored?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: It is largely clinical — mark the erythema margin and review; do bloods/cultures if the patient is unwell, and consider Doppler for possible DVT or joint aspiration for possible gout.
Antibiotics (oral or IV depending on severity, e.g. Eron class), limb elevation, and treatment of the portal of entry (e.g. tinea pedis).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: How should bilateral venous eczema misdiagnosed as cellulitis be managed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: With emollients, a topical steroid and compression — not antibiotics.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.front: What is the significance of periorbital/orbital cellulitis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spre.back: It threatens the eye (proptosis, painful eye movements, reduced acuity) and needs urgent imaging and IV antibiotics.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: How should a skin lump be assessed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: Describe its site, size, shape, surface, consistency, mobility, tethering and overlying skin, plus the history of growth — and decide whether it is benign or worrying.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: What features make a skin/subcutaneous lump a red flag for malignancy?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: Hard, fixed/tethered, deep to the fascia, larger than 5 cm, growing, painful or ulcerating — suggesting sarcoma, skin cancer or metastasis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: What is the quick bedside sign of an epidermoid (sebaceous) cyst?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: A mobile dermal lump with a central punctum; it can become infected or discharge keratin.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: What is the 'slip sign' and which lump shows it?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: The edge of the lump slips away from a palpating finger; it is characteristic of a lipoma (soft, mobile, lobulated, benign).
A firm dermal nodule dimples inward when the surrounding skin is pinched — typical of a benign dermatofibroma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: What is a Sister Mary Joseph nodule?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: A firm nodule at the umbilicus that represents a cutaneous metastasis from an intra-abdominal (or pelvic) malignancy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: What is the appropriate pathway for a soft-tissue lump that is >5 cm, deep, fixed or growing?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: An urgent MRI and biopsy along the sarcoma pathway (do not simply shell it out).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: How can skin cancers present as lumps/nodules?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: A pearly/telangiectatic nodule (BCC), a keratotic/ulcerating nodule (SCC), or a changing/pigmented nodule (melanoma, including amelanotic).
Firm dermal nodules, often with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) and lymphadenopathy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: How is a benign lipoma managed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: Reassurance and safety-netting; imaging or removal if it is large, deep, growing or symptomatic.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.front: What investigations help characterise a soft-tissue lump?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodul.back: Ultrasound for a soft-tissue lump, and urgent MRI plus biopsy for red-flag features; dermoscopy and biopsy for suspected skin cancer.
A rapidly growing, friable red nodule that bleeds easily, often after minor trauma; it is benign but usually needs removal to stop bleeding and confirm the diagnosis (amelanotic melanoma is a mimic).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: Transient reddening of the skin (typically the face, neck and upper chest) due to cutaneous vasodilation.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.front: What is the key clinical question in assessing flushing?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: What company does it keep? Associated symptoms (diarrhoea, wheeze, hypertension, headache, urticaria) point to serious secretory causes, whereas isolated flushing is usually benign.
Emotion, heat, exercise, fever, hot drinks, spicy food and alcohol, the menopause (hot flushes), rosacea, and drugs (niacin, calcium-channel blockers, nitrates).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.front: What is the classic triad of carcinoid syndrome?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: Flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze (with right-sided heart valve disease), from a neuroendocrine tumour with hepatic metastases; confirmed by urinary 5-HIAA and chromogranin A.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.front: How does phaeochromocytoma present with flushing?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: Paroxysmal flushing with hypertension, throbbing headache, sweating and palpitations (often with pallor); confirmed by plasma/urinary metanephrines.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.front: How does systemic mastocytosis present, and how is it confirmed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: Flushing, urticaria pigmentosa and anaphylaxis; confirmed by a raised serum tryptase.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.front: Which endocrine malignancy causes flushing and is associated with MEN2?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (with flushing, diarrhoea and a neck lump), confirmed by a raised calcitonin.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.front: How does flushing feature in anaphylaxis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: Flushing occurs with urticaria and airway/breathing/circulatory compromise (wheeze, stridor, hypotension); treatment is immediate IM adrenaline.
Niacin, calcium-channel blockers and nitrates; and alcohol combined with disulfiram or chlorpropamide.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.front: How is menopausal flushing diagnosed and managed?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: Clinically (hot flushes, night sweats, menstrual change around age 50; FSH may support it), and managed with lifestyle measures and/or HRT.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.front: Which biochemical test matches each secretory cause of flushing?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing.back: Carcinoid → urinary 5-HIAA; phaeochromocytoma → metanephrines; mastocytosis → serum tryptase; medullary thyroid cancer → calcitonin.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: A 5-year-old is febrile, drowsy and has a rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. What is the immediate priority?
options: Give immediate parenteral antibiotics and resuscitate
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: A febrile, unwell child with a non-blanching purpuric rash has meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise; give immediate antibiotics and resuscitate.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: A patient develops a painful rash with mouth and eye erosions, blisters and skin peeling two weeks after starting lamotrigine. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: A painful rash with mucosal erosions, blistering and skin detachment after a drug is SJS/TEN; stop the drug and refer urgently.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: A patient develops widespread urticaria with lip swelling, wheeze and hypotension minutes after a bee sting. What is the immediate treatment?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: Urticaria with airway/breathing/circulatory compromise is anaphylaxis, treated with immediate IM adrenaline.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: A patient has redness and scaling affecting almost the entire skin surface with shivering and tachycardia. What is this presentation called?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: Erythema over >90% of the body surface with systemic upset is erythroderma, a dermatological emergency.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: Which single bedside manoeuvre best distinguishes purpura from an erythematous rash?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: Pressing a glass slide over the rash: purpura does not blanch, whereas an erythematous rash blanches.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: An atopic child has a chronic, intensely itchy, ill-defined rash in the antecubital and popliteal flexures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: A chronic itchy flexural rash in an atopic child is atopic eczema.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: A patient has well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale over the elbows, knees and scalp. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and scalp are typical of psoriasis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: A patient with atopic eczema suddenly develops clusters of monomorphic punched-out erosions with fever. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: Monomorphic punched-out erosions on eczema with systemic upset indicate eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV), needing aciclovir.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: Which feature most strongly suggests necrotising fasciitis rather than simple cellulitis?
options: Pain out of proportion to the skin signs with rapid spread
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread and systemic toxicity suggest necrotising fasciitis, a surgical emergency.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: A widespread rash with fever, facial swelling, lymphadenopathy and eosinophilia develops 4 weeks after starting allopurinol. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: Rash with fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and organ involvement weeks after a drug is DRESS syndrome.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: Which description of urticaria is correct?
options: Transient itchy wheals, each lasting less than 24 hours
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: Urticaria consists of transient, migratory, itchy wheals, each individual lesion lasting under 24 hours.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.question: What is the correct overall approach to an undifferentiated rash?
options: Name the rash immediately from its appearance
Screen for emergencies, then describe morphology, distribution and time course
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash.explanation: First screen for the dermatological emergencies, then systematically describe the rash (morphology, distribution, time course) to reach a diagnosis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: A 28-year-old has generalised itch, drenching night sweats, weight loss and rubbery cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Itch with B symptoms and rubbery lymphadenopathy strongly suggests Hodgkin lymphoma.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: A patient has itch, jaundice, pale stools and dark urine with a raised ALP and GGT. What is the mechanism of the itch?
options: Retained bile salts in the skin (cholestasis)
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Cholestasis causes retention of bile salts that deposit in the skin and provoke itch.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: A 34-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation has intense itching of the palms and soles with no rash and raised bile acids. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Third-trimester itch of the palms/soles without a rash and raised bile acids is obstetric cholestasis, which carries a fetal risk.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: A patient on haemodialysis complains of persistent generalised itch with normal-looking skin apart from scratch marks. What is the cause?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Generalised itch in advanced CKD/dialysis with only excoriations is uraemic pruritus.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: A patient reports intense itching every time after a warm bath, and has a ruddy face and a haematocrit of 0.57. What is the likely diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Aquagenic pruritus (itch after a warm bath) with plethora and a high haematocrit suggests polycythaemia vera.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: A family all develop intense nocturnal itch, and the index patient has burrows in the finger webs. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Burrows in the finger webs with itchy household contacts indicate scabies.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: An older adult has painless jaundice, weight loss and troublesome itch. Which serious cause must be excluded?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss and itch may be pancreatic or biliary cancer.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: Which single investigation panel best begins the work-up of itch without a rash?
options: FBC, ferritin, U&E, LFTs, TFTs (± LDH/HIV)
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Bloods (FBC, ferritin, U&E/eGFR, LFTs, TFTs, and LDH/HIV as indicated) screen for the systemic causes of itch without a rash.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: An elderly man has generalised itch that is worse in winter, with dry, scaly skin and no other features. What is the most likely cause?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Dry, scaly skin worse in winter in an elderly patient is xerosis, the commonest cause of itch in this group.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: A middle-aged woman has itch, fatigue and a cholestatic LFT pattern with positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Cholestatic itch with anti-mitochondrial antibodies in a middle-aged woman indicates primary biliary cholangitis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: Which symptomatic measure is appropriate for most causes of pruritus while investigating?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Emollients, cooling measures and antihistamines relieve itch while the underlying cause is treated.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.question: Itch without a primary rash should always prompt what key action?
options: A search for a systemic cause (bloods) and red flags
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus.explanation: Itch without a rash warrants screening bloods for systemic disease and a search for red flags (nodes, jaundice, weight loss).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: A febrile, unwell patient has a rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. What is the immediate priority?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Fever with a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash in an unwell patient is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise; give antibiotics immediately.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: A child has palpable purpura over the buttocks and legs with abdominal pain, arthralgia and haematuria. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Palpable purpura on the buttocks/legs with abdominal pain, arthralgia and nephritis is Henoch-Schönlein purpura (an IgA small-vessel vasculitis).

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: Which feature of a purpuric rash most specifically indicates a small-vessel vasculitis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Palpable purpura indicates inflammation of the vessel wall (leukocytoclastic vasculitis); flat purpura does not.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: A patient develops net-like, angulated, black necrotic purpura a few days after starting warfarin. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Retiform necrotic purpura days after starting warfarin is warfarin skin necrosis, an occlusive process.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: Which investigation should be prioritised in a patient with palpable purpura and haematuria?
options: Skin biopsy with ANCA and urinalysis
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Palpable purpura with renal involvement needs a skin biopsy plus ANCA and urinalysis to characterise the vasculitis and assess the kidneys.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: A septic patient develops widespread retiform purpura with skin necrosis, low platelets, low fibrinogen and a high D-dimer. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Retiform necrotic purpura with consumptive coagulopathy in a septic patient is DIC/purpura fulminans.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: A patient has non-palpable purpura and an isolated platelet count of 15 but is otherwise well. What is the likely cause?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Non-palpable purpura with isolated thrombocytopenia in a well patient suggests immune thrombocytopenia.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: A patient with fever, a new murmur, splinter haemorrhages and scattered purpura most likely has which underlying diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Fever with a new murmur, splinter haemorrhages and purpura points to infective endocarditis.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: An elderly patient on long-term steroids has non-palpable purpura confined to the backs of the hands, with a normal FBC. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Non-palpable purpura on the extensor hands/forearms with normal blood counts in an elderly or steroid-treated patient is senile/steroid purpura.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: Which morphology of purpura should prompt an urgent coagulation screen and search for a thrombotic driver?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Retiform/necrotic purpura reflects vessel occlusion and warrants a coagulation screen and a hunt for a thrombotic cause.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: What is the correct first-line blood investigation to triage non-palpable purpura?
options: FBC with blood film (and coagulation screen)
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: FBC with blood film (plus a coagulation screen) triages non-palpable purpura into thrombocytopenic, coagulopathic or fragile-vessel causes.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.question: On palpating a purpuric rash, how does the finding guide you?
options: Palpable = vasculitis; flat = platelet/vessel; retiform = occlusion
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash.explanation: Palpable purpura is vasculitis, flat purpura is a platelet/vessel problem, and retiform/necrotic purpura is occlusive.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.question: A patient develops widespread wheals with lip swelling, wheeze and hypotension minutes after eating peanuts. What is the immediate treatment?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.explanation: Urticaria with airway/breathing/circulatory compromise is anaphylaxis, treated with immediate IM adrenaline.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.question: Which feature confirms that a raised itchy lesion is an urticarial wheal rather than something more sinister?
options: Each individual lesion lasts less than 24 hours and blanches
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.explanation: An urticarial wheal is transient (each lesion less than 24 hours), blanching and migratory.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.question: A patient has weals that each last more than 24 hours, are painful and leave bruising. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.explanation: Weals lasting over 24 hours that are painful and leave bruising indicate urticarial vasculitis, needing a skin biopsy.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.question: A patient on ramipril develops recurrent swelling of the lips and tongue without any weals or itch. What is the cause?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.explanation: Angioedema without weals in a patient on an ACE inhibitor is ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema; stop the drug.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.question: Which investigation should be checked in recurrent angioedema without weals and a family history?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.explanation: Hereditary angioedema is diagnosed by a low C1-esterase inhibitor and low C4.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.question: A child develops crops of transient itchy wheals a few days into a viral upper respiratory infection. What is the likely cause?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.explanation: Post-viral urticaria is the commonest cause of acute urticaria in children.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.question: A patient has daily itchy wheals for 3 months with no identifiable trigger. What is the diagnosis?
signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.explanation: Daily weals for more than 6 weeks with no external trigger is chronic spontaneous urticaria.

signs__DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria.question: Linear wheals appear wherever a patient scratches or strokes their skin. What is this called?
